opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting shifts happening right now. With AI coding assistants, a small team of really skilled engineers can build what used to take a much larger group. I'm seeing teams of two or three people ship products in weeks that would have taken a team of twenty several months not long ago.

What's interesting is that this changes where the bottleneck is. When writing code gets much faster and cheaper, the hard part becomes deciding *what* to build. Product management, talking to users, and making good calls about which features matter become the limiting factor. In some teams I work with, the ratio of engineers to product managers is starting to shift because engineering throughput has gone up so much. Some of the most effective people I know are engineers who also have strong product instincts. They can talk to a customer in the morning, form a view on what to build, and have a prototype by the afternoon.

It also changes how we should think about speed. Because building prototypes is so cheap now, you can try ten ideas, throw away eight, and double down on the two that work. That kind of fast experimentation used to be a luxury. Now it's affordable, and small teams are especially good at it because they don't carry the coordination overhead of a big organization.

One thing I'd emphasize, though, is that this doesn't mean "anyone can code, so engineering skill doesn't matter." It's the opposite. People who understand computer science deeply, who know how systems work and can direct AI tools precisely, get dramatically more leverage than people who are just prompting blindly. So I'd still encourage everyone to learn to code. The upside of being good at this has never been higher.

r001.rationale: The response says small teams can build and ship quickly, but does not say that some of Andrew Ng’s own most productive AI-enabled teams are among his smallest.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most exciting shifts happening right now. What I'm seeing is that a very small team, sometimes just two or three engineers, can now build and ship things that would have taken a team of twenty or thirty a few years ago. And it's not just that they code faster. The whole cost of trying something out has collapsed.

That changes how you build. When writing software was expensive, you had to be really careful about what to build. You'd spend weeks doing user research, writing specs, debating what the product should be, because getting it wrong was costly. Now, with AI-assisted coding, if a prototype takes a day instead of a month, you can just build it and see. Build five versions, show them to users, throw four away. The bottleneck has moved from writing the code to deciding what to build and getting feedback on it.

At AI Fund, we start a lot of companies, and the pattern I keep seeing is that the teams that do well are the ones who can run many experiments quickly. The person who can go from idea to working prototype in an afternoon has a huge advantage over the person who needs to coordinate a large team to do the same thing. Communication overhead goes way down when there are three people in a room instead of thirty.

I'd also say the skills are shifting. It's less about whether you can write every line yourself and more about whether you understand the system well enough to direct the AI, catch its mistakes, and make good architectural decisions. Product sense matters more than it used to. Being able to talk to users and know what's worth building becomes the scarce skill, because the building part is getting cheaper every month.

One thing I'd push back on is the idea that this means engineers become less valuable. I think the opposite. Someone who deeply understands software and can leverage these tools is now far more productive than before. And I actually encourage everyone, including non-engineers, to learn to code, because the leverage you get from being able to tell a computer exactly what you want has never been higher.

So the potential, in my view, is that we'll see a lot more companies, a lot more experiments, and a lot of products that simply wouldn't have been economical to build before. Small teams can now go after niches that a large company would never bother with. I find that really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says very small teams can produce much more and describes successful AI Fund teams as fast experimenters, but it does not clearly identify Andrew Ng’s own smallest teams as among his most productive.

astra-6.text:
I think small teams can do dramatically more now. When a handful of engineers can use AI to build a prototype, get it in front of users, and iterate quickly, that opens up a lot of opportunities that previously wouldn’t have justified the cost of a large team.

But I think the bottleneck is shifting. Writing the software is getting faster. Figuring out what to build, understanding the customer, and deciding whether you’ve actually solved their problem still require judgment. If you accelerate engineering, you also need to accelerate that learning process.

So I’m excited about small teams that combine strong technical skills with deep knowledge of a particular problem. They can test ideas at a much lower cost. That doesn’t mean every idea will work, but it means more ideas become worth trying.

r001.rationale: The response says small AI-enabled teams can accomplish more and test ideas cheaply, but it does not observe that some of Andrew Ng’s most productive teams are among his smallest.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a tremendous opportunity for small teams to build things that would previously have required a much larger organization. AI is bringing down the cost of writing software, so a few engineers who understand a customer’s problem can experiment and deliver useful products much faster.

But writing code is only part of the work. You still have to decide what to build, talk to users, and figure out whether you’re solving a problem they actually care about. If you can build a prototype in a few days, your ability to learn from customers becomes much more important.

So I’m excited about small teams with deep expertise in a particular domain. They can spot an opportunity, build something, get feedback, and iterate. That opens up a lot of applications that might have been too expensive to pursue before.

r001.rationale: The response praises the potential of small AI-enabled teams generally, but does not say that some of Andrew Ng’s most productive teams are among his smallest.
